sentences.text: Infernogallus was a small caenagnathid estimated at about 12 kilograms in body mass.
It possessed a toothless beak, a modestly crested skull, a long neck, a short torso, and elongated legs, giving it a silhouette reminiscent of a bird.
The eye socket occupied nearly 40% of the total skull length, while the infratemporal opening was only about a quarter of the orbit's diameter.
A notably large pterygoid shelf filled most of the oral cavity, and its vertebrae were pneumatic, containing extensive air spaces.
The ulna was bowed rather than straight, a condition that differs from that of heyuannine oviraptorids.
The second metacarpal was the longest bone in the hand and bore a shallow ridge absent in other caenagnathids.
Its cochlea was relatively short, suggesting reduced auditory sensitivity compared with other theropods.
The skull of Infernogallus is the first nearly complete and articulated caenagnathid skull ever discovered.
Its skull and muscle arrangement resemble that of Pesquet's parrot, a modern frugivorous bird.
The holotype, designated Infernogallus jamesi, consists of a partially articulated skull and skeleton together with several isolated cranial bones.
Five specimens have been recovered from Hell Creek outcrops across Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota.
The generic name combines the Latin words for “Hell” (īnfernus) and “chicken” (gallus) to reference its Hell Creek origin and bird-like appearance.
The specific epithet jamesi honors James William Boyd, the grandfather of co-author Clint Boyd.
The study describing Infernogallus was published in Nature Communications in 2026.
The animal was at least six, probably seven, years old when it died, having reached full adult size.
Its jaw muscles were enlarged in the palate and reduced in the temporal region, indicating a weaker bite force than non-caenagnathid oviraptorosaurs.
Highly textured occlusal surfaces would have allowed effective crushing and shearing of soft foods.
A strong tongue is inferred from the muscle insertion site on the mandible.
No gastroliths were found in the articulated body cavity, implying they were not used in digestion.
The animal likely consumed a soft, non-fibrous diet that required oral processing rather than reliance on gastroliths.
Jaw modifications permitted extensive front-to-back mandible movement and occlusion of ridges and grooves for processing soft food.
Researchers propose that caenagnathids, including Infernogallus, were specialized herbivores that ate fleshy angiosperm fruits.
Infernogallus jamesi is named as a new genus and species of diminutive caenagnathid oviraptorosaur.
It shows a unique adductor musculature organization convergent with that of living frugivorous parrots.
Fossil evidence suggests caenagnathids, including Infernogallus, originated soon after the appearance of angiosperm fruits such as drupes.
The connection between dinosaur diversification and the rise of angiosperm fruits remains a topic of debate among scientists.
